en.title: Ti West's 'Ebenezer' Casts Johnny Depp in a Dark, Freddy Krueger-Inspired Scrooge
en.summary: Director Ti West is reimagining 'A Christmas Carol' with a gritty, horror-tinged vision, starring Johnny Depp. The film draws inspiration from classic chilling adaptations and mid-century British thrillers.
en.body:
After delving into the dark heart of horror with his acclaimed trilogy of **X**, **Pearl**, and **MaXXXine**, director **Ti West** sought a new creative path. His latest project, **Ebenezer**, ventures into the familiar territory of Charles Dickens' **A Christmas Carol**, but with a distinctly Westian sensibility – one that promises to be far from your typical holiday fare.

West's approach to Dickens' classic tale is deeply personal, informed by childhood memories of a particular adaptation. "As a kid, I watched the George C. Scott version, and Marley really freaked me out," West explains. "I have this visceral memory of one of the earliest horror-ish things that I watched being A Christmas Carol, and I got a little scared in a couple parts… So when I was talking about making the movie to the studio, I was like, ‘It’s hard-PG.’ I want to make something like the movies I grew up on that you were allowed to watch as a kid but occasionally pushed it just a little too far."

This desire to tap into a more unsettling, yet still accessible, cinematic experience is evident in the film's casting and aesthetic. **Johnny Depp** takes on the role of Ebenezer Scrooge, a choice that immediately signals this won't be a straightforward interpretation. The visual language of **Ebenezer** deliberately evokes the mid-20th century British chillers, reminiscent of Hammer Studios' lurid Victorian horror cycles. This deliberate stylistic choice, coupled with the film's intended "hard-PG" rating, suggests a darker, more atmospheric take on Scrooge's journey than many familiar adaptations.

## A 'Gray' Scrooge for Modern Audiences

West's vision for Scrooge is anything but black and white. He aims to create a character that, while flawed and perhaps even frightening, possesses a complexity that resonates with contemporary audiences. This isn't the cartoonish miser of some adaptations, nor is it the outright villain of others. Instead, West is crafting a "gray" Scrooge, a figure whose struggles and eventual transformation might feel more relatable and earned. The inspiration for the darker elements, including a potential nod to **Freddy Krueger**, hints at a psychological depth that could elevate the narrative beyond a simple ghost story.

## What This Means for Fans

For fans of **Ti West**, this project represents an exciting departure while retaining his signature thematic interests. His ability to weave intricate narratives with a keen understanding of cinematic history has garnered critical acclaim, even attracting the admiration of **Martin Scorsese**. The prospect of seeing **Johnny Depp** in a role that allows for both gravitas and a touch of the macabre, under West's direction, is a significant draw. This reimagining taps into a growing appetite for genre-bending stories that offer something beyond the expected, promising a holiday film that might just give you chills for all the right reasons.

## What's Next

Details regarding the release date and further casting for **Ebenezer** have not yet been announced. Fans eager for **Ti West**'s latest work will be keeping a close watch for future updates on this ambitious adaptation.

After writing and directing a decades-spanning trilogy of horror and cinematic homages via X , Pearl , and MaXXXine —films that count Martin Scorsese among their fans—the New England filmmaker needed to step away from the genre. If perhaps by only a few inches. “Everybody loves IP, and I was like, ‘Well, what IP do I really love?’” West muses when we catch up with the filmmaker while he’s on a whirlwind press tour for Ebenezer , a thoroughly reimagined take on Charles Dickens’ classic A Christmas Carol . By virtue of the film he’s promoting, it’s obvious where his nostalgia took him, albeit the filmmaker admits that his own memories of watching a specific 1984 TV movie adaptation of Dickens informed just how dark and horror-twinged he wanted to take the tale of Ebenezer Scrooge. “As a kid, I watched the George C. Scott version, and Marley really freaked me out,” West explains. “I have this visceral memory of one of the earliest horror-ish things that I watched being A Christmas Carol , and I got a little scared in a couple parts… So when I was talking about making the movie to the studio, I was like, ‘It’s hard-PG.’ I want to make something like the movies I grew up on that you were allowed to watch as a kid but occasionally pushed it just a little too far.” Right down to casting the once and future genre-connoisseur Johnny Depp as a different take on Scrooge, West’s Ebenezer feels a world apart from Disney or Muppets interpretations, or even the slightly more sinister George C. Scott iteration. Right down to its visual aesthetics and antiquated opening credits sequence, West deliberately evokes the cinematic vernacular of mid-20th century British chillers like Hammer Studios’ cycle of lurid Victorian horror movies. “I think Hammer has just such a pleasing aesthetic to me,” West explains, “The amount of conversations I had about ‘no, no the candle should be really red, or that candle should be really green or really blue.’ When you first put them on set, you’re like, ‘This is preposterous! This is a crazy thing to do,’ but I’m so charmed by the aesthetic of Hammer because there’s a beauty to those movies… they’re somewhat preposterous choices, but they are aesthetically appealing.” They also bring the film in line with a timeless sense of British cinema that West is aiming to evoke in a very familiar tale.
